digest.top_line: NRG-GU005: 5-fx SBRT beats MH-IMRT on 2yr bowel MCID decline (35% vs 44%, p=0.034) but DFS superiority stopped for futility (HR 1.38).
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day, and the read is fractionation, not efficacy: NRG-GU005 buys toxicity with SBRT while 3yr biochemical failure runs 8% vs 4% (p=0.037), and a 10-yr 40 Gy/5 fx cohort shows 90% RFS with two-thirds of relapses after year 5. Head/neck gets its first post-op OCSCC CTV atlas, consensus-only.

sites.intro: Two ultrahypofractionation datasets plus an ARS consensus on salvaging the irradiated gland.

studies.name: SBRT for Prostate Cancer: 10-yr Nonrandomized Cohort (Meier et al.)
studies.tldr: 10-yr RFS 90% overall (94% LR, 86% IR) after 40 Gy/5 fx SBRT, late Gr3 GU 1.4-1.5%, no Gr4-5.
details: 📊 10-yr freedom from biochemical/clinical relapse 92% (87-96) whole group
📊 10-yr freedom from local failure 96% (93-99); LR 98% (95-100), IR 94% (89-99), p=0.12
🔍 Dose 40 Gy/5 fx (8 Gy x5, ~100 Gy EQD2 at a/b=2) on a noncoplanar robotic platform
🔍 Fiducial tracking with translational + rotational intrafractional correction mandatory
🔍 Phase 2 nonrandomized, 21 community/regional/academic sites, N=310 evaluable, median f/u 9 yr
🔍 Eligibility: LR T1b-T2a GS6 PSA<=10, or IR T1b-T2b GS7 or PSA 10-20; ADT not allowed; prostate volume up to 100 cc
📊 10-yr Gr2+ toxicity 2.1% GI and 14% GU; 4 pts had 5 Gr3 events, all GU; none after year 5
🔗 IR result compares favorably to the 74-78% 10-yr RFS with dose-escalated EBRT in RTOG 0126 (authors' comparison)
🔗 Toxicity similar to Fuller's CyberKnife SBRT trial; higher in PACE-B SBRT arm and PATRIOT, both largely conventional-linac delivered
⚠️ Grade group 3 was the only unfavorable risk factor independently predicting 10-yr biochemical/clinical failure on multivariate analysis
⚠️ Two-thirds of relapses occurred between 5-10 yr, so 5-yr series systematically understate failure
⚠️ Nonrandomized, sponsor-funded (Accuray), physician-reported CTCAE v3 toxicity only, no patient-reported outcomes in source

verdict.rationale: Nonrandomized phase 2, single-platform, no comparator arm; extends 5-yr data the field already acts on rather than testing SBRT against EBRT.
verdict.audience: Localized low- or intermediate-risk prostate CA, no ADT, prostate volume <=100 cc

studies.significance: Two-thirds of relapses fell between 5 and 10 yr, so every 5-yr SBRT series (including PACE-B) is reading an immature curve. The unfavorable IR subgroup separated at 77% vs 92% (p=0.002) with ADT prohibited, which is where the trial actually moves a decision: whether to add ADT rather than whether to use 40 Gy/5 fx.
studies.monday_clinic: In unfavorable intermediate-risk disease, particularly grade group 3, this argues the ADT question stays open at 10 yr; in low-risk and favorable IR pts it supports 40 Gy in 5 fractions as monotherapy without hormone therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Investigator-initiated **phase 2 nonrandomized** trial across **21 sites** (community, regional, academic), accrual January 2008 to April 2010. **N=310 evaluable** (172 LR, 138 IR), median age 68, **median follow-up 9 yr**. Kaplan-Meier estimates with log-rank comparison of LR vs IR.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **LR:** T1b-T2a, Gleason 6, PSA <=10 ng/ml. **IR:** T1b-T2b, Gleason 7 with PSA <=10, or Gleason 6 with PSA >10 to 20. Central pathology review; IR split favorable vs unfavorable by MSK classification. Prostate volume up to 100 cc allowed; prior TURP and baseline AUA score were **not** exclusions.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **40 Gy in five fractions** (8 Gy x 5, equivalent to 100 Gy at 2 Gy/fx assuming a/b=2) on a **noncoplanar robotic platform** with real-time motion management. Fiducial tracking plus **translational and rotational** intrafractional correction were mandatory. **Androgen suppression was not allowed**, so the entire result is RT monotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Relapse-free survival (biochemical or clinical failure, or any salvage/antiandrogen/systemic therapy), overall survival, freedom from local failure, and late toxicity (>90 d) by **CTCAE v3**. Biochemical failure defined as **nadir+2**, unless followed by a new nadir.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 10-yr OS **84%** (76-91); RFS **92%** (87-96) whole group; freedom from local failure **96%** (93-99). The only statistically separated comparison was favorable vs unfavorable IR (**92% vs 77%, p=0.002**); LR vs IR did not reach significance for RFS (p=0.19), OS (p=0.22), or local failure (p=0.12).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Four pts had five grade 3 toxicities, **all GU**, and **none after year 5**. 10-yr cumulative grade 3 rates **1.4%** (0-3.4) LR and **1.5%** (0-3.7) IR, far under the prespecified 10% threshold. **No grade 4-5 events.** 10-yr grade 2+ was **2.1% GI** and **14% GU**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PACE-B established SBRT as noninferior to conventionally fractionated EBRT at 5 yr but stops there; this extends the curve to 10. The authors read their IR RFS against the **74-78%** 10-yr RFS of dose-escalated EBRT in **RTOG 0126**, and note toxicity ran higher in the PACE-B SBRT arm and **PATRIOT**, both predominantly conventional-linac. **MIRAGE** is invoked as independent support that intrafractional motion management lowers toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents organ-confined low-risk and intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with robotic SBRT and no ADT. Does not represent high-risk disease, node-positive disease, prostate volumes above 100 cc, or delivery without fiducial-based intrafractional tracking.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The platform is not incidental: the authors attribute their low toxicity to mandatory fiducial tracking with rotational correction, so the 1.5% grade 3 rate is a claim about robotic delivery, not about 40 Gy/5 fx generally. The trial was funded by the device manufacturer and one author consults for it. Toxicity is physician-reported CTCAE v3 only, which systematically underreads GU and GI symptoms relative to patient-reported instruments.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The durable finding is the **timing** of failure: two-thirds of relapses occurred between 5 and 10 yr, so the 5-yr endpoints that currently anchor SBRT practice are immature. **Grade group 3** was the only independent predictor of 10-yr failure on multivariate analysis, which the authors read as an argument for considering ADT in that subset rather than as a reason to change dose.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report is not that SBRT works, which PACE-B settled at 5 yr, but that it shows how much of the failure curve the 5-yr literature has been missing. Two-thirds of relapses in this cohort occurred between years 5 and 10. That single observation reframes every SBRT series a radiation oncologist currently quotes to a patient in clinic, including PACE-B's own 5-yr relapse data, as an estimate taken before most of the events have happened. It is also the reason a 10-yr nonrandomized cohort earns attention it would not otherwise get: no randomized SBRT trial has follow-up long enough to answer the question, so the comparison available is this cohort against historical dose-escalated EBRT.

That comparison should be read with the usual discount. The authors set their 86% 10-yr intermediate-risk RFS against the 74-78% reported with dose-escalated EBRT in RTOG 0126 and note it looks more favorable. RTOG 0126 accrued a different era, a different staging workup, and a different definition of intermediate risk, and this trial required central pathologic review while excluding anyone who needed androgen suppression. A cohort assembled that way is selected toward better outcomes independent of the radiation delivered. The honest read is that the SBRT curve is at least not worse over a decade, which given the fractionation convenience is the practically relevant conclusion, not that ultrahypofractionation has beaten dose-escalated EBRT.

The toxicity result carries a more specific and more transferable caveat, and it is a technical one. Grade 3 late toxicity was 1.4% and 1.5%, all GU, with nothing new after year 5, and no grade 4-5 events at all. The authors do not attribute this to the dose; they attribute it to delivery, noting that fiducial tracking with both translational and rotational intrafractional correction was mandatory, that PACE-B and PATRIOT reported higher toxicity with predominantly conventional-linac delivery, and that PACE-B's own subset treated on CyberKnife did better than its linac subset. MIRAGE, which randomized margin reduction under MRI guidance, points the same direction. So the number a reader should carry out of this paper is conditional: 40 Gy in five fractions with real-time intrafractional motion management produced these rates. A department delivering the same prescription with pretreatment imaging and standard margins has not been shown to reproduce them. Working against the toxicity figures generally is that they are physician-reported CTCAE v3, which reads GU and GI symptoms less sensitively than patient-reported instruments, and that the sponsor manufactures the platform being credited.

Where this changes a decision is the unfavorable intermediate-risk subgroup. RFS was 92% for favorable and 77% for unfavorable IR, the only comparison in the trial to separate statistically (p=0.002), and grade group 3 was the only factor independently predicting 10-yr failure on multivariate analysis. Because androgen suppression was prohibited, this is a clean look at what SBRT alone delivers in that group, and 77% at 10 yr is the number to weigh against the toxicity and quality-of-life cost of adding ADT. The trial cannot answer whether ADT would close that gap; it establishes the size of the gap that a trial would have to close. For the low-risk and favorable IR patient, meanwhile, the argument for monotherapy is now supported by durable rather than interim data, and the residual uncertainty is mostly about whether the delivery platform travels.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Two-thirds of relapses fell between 5 and 10 yr, so 5-yr SBRT series read an immature curve. The 1.4-1.5% grade 3 rate is conditional on mandatory fiducial tracking with rotational intrafractional correction, not on 40 Gy/5 fx alone, which gates whether it transfers to a linac-based practice.

open_questions: Does ADT close the 77% vs 92% unfavorable IR relapse gap
Do non-robotic SBRT platforms reproduce the 1.5% late grade 3 rate

studies.name: American Radium Society AUC: Local Intraprostatic Recurrence
studies.tldr: Consensus AUC: PSMA PET + mpMRI, mandatory targeted AND systematic biopsy, then reirradiation over RP for isolated intraprostatic radiorecurrence.

details.text: 📊 Panel recommendations by topic (modified Delphi, 12 voting members)

rows: PSMA PET + mpMRI to exclude metastatic disease and map local extent
Required before salvage; both targeted AND systematic
Reirradiation usually appropriate; cryo/HIFU may be appropriate
Not recommended for confirmed local recurrence, any agent or duration
Short 4-6 mo LHRH agonist appropriate; novel agents not endorsed
Focal if mpMRI + systematic biopsy concordant; whole-gland if discordant

details.text: 📐 Reirradiation dose schemas the panel considers acceptable
subdetails: SBRT 34-40 Gy in 5 fx (34 Gy/5 whole-gland Fuller series; 40 Gy/5 focal MTD)
HDR 27 Gy in 2 fx, 32 Gy in 4 fx, or 36 Gy in 6 fx over 2 implants
LDR minimum target dose 140 Gy (I-125) or 120 Gy (Pd-103), per RTOG 0526

details.text: 📊 MASTER meta-analysis toxicity, RP as reference (adjusted rates)

details: 📊 MASTER pooled 150 studies, 11 322 pts; adjusted 5-yr RFS 50-60%, no survival difference between any modality and RP
🔍 Biopsy mandate is driven by radiographic false positives: PSMA PET false-positive rate 8% in Fendler (n=635), post-RT change the usual culprit
🔍 Systematic biopsy cannot be dropped: FORECAST secondary analysis found up to 59% of true radiorecurrences would be occult with MRI-targeted cores alone
📐 mpMRI alone is a poor gate: sensitivity 94% (88-98%) but specificity 18% (7-35%) vs systematic biopsy reference (FORECAST, n=155)
🔗 RTOG 0526 (LDR salvage, n=92) reported DFS 61% at 5 yr and 33% at 10 yr with 10-yr local failure 5%, published after MASTER closed
⚠️ Evidence base predates PSMA PET, so the very patients this guideline defines (local-only) could not be identified in the trials it cites
⚠️ Evidence limited to prior conventionally fractionated EBRT; prior brachytherapy pts were excluded and moderate/ultrahypofractionated first courses are unstudied for salvage
⚠️ No consensus on second salvage (variant 4), on castrate-resistant local recurrence (variant 3), or on modality after prior grade 3 toxicity (variant 5)

verdict.rationale: ARS appropriate use criteria, modified Delphi across 12 panelists. Output is recommendation strength per variant, not an efficacy result; most underlying evidence retrospective.
verdict.audience: Biopsy-confirmed local-only intraprostatic recurrence after definitive EBRT

studies.significance: The volumetric rule is the operational content: focal salvage when mpMRI and systematic biopsy agree on location, whole-gland when they disagree or the lesion sits away from the index lesion. Panel puts SBRT and HDR ahead of RP on therapeutic ratio (severe GU 5.6% and 9.6% vs 20%), with a short 4-6 mo LHRH agonist for radiosensitization.
studies.monday_clinic: In a man with rising PSA after definitive EBRT and PSMA PET showing prostate-only avidity, this supports biopsying (targeted plus systematic) before committing to salvage and favors reirradiation over prostatectomy or ADT alone; it does not cover prior brachytherapy or prior hypofractionated courses.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ARS Genitourinary AUC, **12 voting panelists** across radiation oncology, urology and medical oncology. PRISMA literature search of PubMed and Embase run **28 June 2022**, four separate searches for four topics, then **two rounds of modified Delphi voting** with RAND disagreement methodology.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Scope is deliberately narrow: **tier A failure**, isolated intraprostatic radiorecurrence after definitive RT, in patients who want curative-intent local salvage. Tier B (nodal) and tier C (distant) are out of scope, and **prior brachytherapy patients were excluded** from the evidence synthesis.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Acceptable reirradiation schemas: **36 Gy/6 fx** EBRT (GETUG-AFU 31), **SBRT 34-40 Gy/5 fx**, **HDR 27 Gy/2 fx**, LDR **140 Gy I-125 or 120 Gy Pd-103** (RTOG 0526). GETUG-AFU 31 defines GTV by mpMRI plus choline PET with a **5-7 mm CTV margin bound by the capsule**. F-SHARP is testing 1-2 fraction HDR up to 30 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: No efficacy endpoint. The output is an **appropriateness rating per clinical variant** within each of four topics (staging, salvage modality, hormonal therapy, target volume), with disagreement classified by RAND criteria rather than measured against an outcome.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Panel converged strongly on staging and biopsy, and on reirradiation as the salvage with the best therapeutic ratio. **Disagreement persisted** on short-PSA-doubling-time recurrence, castrate-resistant local recurrence, second salvage, and salvage after prior grade 3 toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The salvage-modality position rests on the **MASTER meta-analysis** (150 studies, 11 322 pts), where adjusted 5-yr RFS was 50-60% with **no survival difference** between modalities but severe GU toxicity of 20% after RP vs 5.6-9.6% after RT salvage. RTOG 0526 reported after MASTER closed and adds prospective phase 2 support for LDR: **5-yr DFS 61%, 10-yr local failure 5%**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with biopsy-confirmed local-only intraprostatic recurrence after conventionally fractionated definitive EBRT who want curative-intent salvage. Does not represent prior brachytherapy, prior moderate or ultrahypofractionated RT, nodal or distant failure, or men not seeking local salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The workup the guideline mandates (PSMA PET) postdates nearly all the evidence it cites, so the trials could not isolate the local-only population the recommendations govern. No high-quality study met inclusion for topics 3 or 4, meaning the hormonal and volumetric recommendations are **expert opinion, not evidence synthesis**. Search date was June 2022, with an acknowledged lag to publication.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document's practical value is that it puts reirradiation ahead of prostatectomy on toxicity grounds while conceding that no modality separates on survival. It also draws a firm line against ADT-alone for confirmed local recurrence, which pushes the decision toward either salvage or surveillance rather than hormonal drift.

studies.interpretation:
This is a positional document, and the position worth arguing about is the demotion of salvage prostatectomy. The panel does not claim reirradiation controls disease better; MASTER found adjusted 5-yr recurrence-free survival of 50% to 60% with no significant survival difference between any modality and RP. The whole case rests on toxicity, where the separation is wide: severe genitourinary toxicity of 20% after RP versus 5.6% after SBRT, 9.6% after HDR and 9.1% after LDR. When efficacy is a wash across modalities, therapeutic ratio is a legitimate tiebreaker, and a radiation oncologist can defend offering reirradiation first on that basis. The caution is that MASTER pooled 150 retrospective series with acknowledged asymmetry of follow-up between older and newer modalities, and salvage RP series skew toward an earlier surgical era. Some of that 20% is technique vintage, not an intrinsic property of the operation, and the comparison cannot separate the two.

The deeper problem is one the panel names itself: the evidence base predates PSMA PET, and PSMA PET is what defines the population these recommendations govern. Liu's cohort of 79 men with exclusively radiorecurrent disease found conventional and PET staging concordant in only 56%, with 34% upstaged. If a third of men previously called local-only actually harbor disease outside the gland, then every historical salvage series is contaminated with patients who were never going to be cured locally, and the reported 50% to 60% recurrence-free survival is a floor rather than an estimate of what modern selection would achieve. That cuts in favor of local salvage, but it also means the panel is recommending an intervention for a population no included study actually enrolled.

The biopsy mandate is the most defensible element and the one most likely to be skipped in practice. mpMRI sensitivity of 94% with specificity of 18% is not a test that can stand alone, and Fendler's 8% false-positive rate on PSMA PET, driven largely by post-treatment change, means imaging concordance is not histologic confirmation. The FORECAST secondary analysis is the sharper point: up to 59% of true radiorecurrences would have been missed had only MRI-targeted cores been taken. Targeted biopsy alone is not a shortcut here, and the panel's discouragement of combined biopsy-and-ablate procedures follows logically from that, even though it costs the patient a second procedure.

Where the guideline is weakest is topics 3 and 4, and it says so. No study met inclusion criteria for either the hormonal question or the focal-versus-whole-gland question, so the 4 to 6 month LHRH agonist recommendation is extrapolated from de novo intermediate-risk data into a setting whose defining feature is that the tumor already survived radiation. The focal-if-concordant rule is a reasonable heuristic rather than a finding. Notably the panel found whole-gland salvage toxicity acceptable in the Fuller series, which weakens the argument for focal treatment on safety grounds and leaves the volumetric choice resting mostly on confidence in localization.

What would have to change for this to be wrong: if prospective PSMA-selected series show reirradiation control rates well above the historical 50% to 60%, the salvage-versus-surveillance calculus shifts materially. If they do not, the panel's stance against ADT-alone becomes harder to hold for men with short doubling times, the exact variant where the panel itself could not reach agreement. The applicability gap also matters practically, since hypofractionation is now standard first-line and no salvage evidence exists after it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Operationally this is a reirradiation guideline: 36 Gy/6 fx, SBRT 34-40 Gy/5 fx, HDR 27 Gy/2 fx, LDR 140 Gy I-125 or 120 Gy Pd-103, with the focal-vs-whole-gland call decided by whether mpMRI and systematic biopsy agree on lesion location. GETUG-AFU 31's 5-7 mm capsule-bound CTV margin is the cited focal template.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: ADT alone is not recommended for confirmed local recurrence regardless of agent or duration; when reirradiation is given, only a short 4-6 mo LHRH agonist is endorsed. Relugolix reached no agreement in this setting, the panel citing HERO's cardiac benefit as an unplanned secondary analysis and PRONOUNCE's failure to replicate it.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Salvage prostatectomy is not excluded but is displaced on therapeutic ratio: severe GU toxicity 20% after RP vs 5.6-9.6% after RT salvage in MASTER, with no survival difference between modalities. The panel also discourages combined biopsy-plus-ablation approaches, since histologic confirmation must precede any salvage.

studies.name: NRG-GU005
studies.tldr: 2yr bowel MCID decline 35% vs 44% (p=0.034) favoring 5-fraction SBRT, but DFS superiority crossed interim futility (HR 1.38).

details.text: 📊 Co-primary and efficacy endpoints, SBRT vs MH-IMRT
🔍 Randomised non-blinded phase 3, N=698 (SBRT 353 / MH-IMRT 345), designed for superiority

details: 📐 SBRT 36.25 Gy/5 fx at 7.25 Gy, 2-3 fx/wk vs 70 Gy/28 fx or 60 Gy/20 fx
🔍 Fiducials, MRI fusion for planning and daily advanced IGRT mandated in both arms

details.text: 📊 Secondary EPIC-26 MCID declines, SBRT vs MH-IMRT

details: ⚠️ Stopped for DFS futility, not harm; no non-inferiority margin was prespecified
📐 Spacer use improved EPIC bowel scores (LS mean -2.81, 95% CI -4.49 to -1.13, p=0.0011)
🔗 vs PACE-B: both show lower urinary incontinence decline with SBRT, MCID definitions differ

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase 3, but the superiority design stopped for DFS futility, so equivalence stays unproven; the QoL co-primary was met and matches PACE-B on continence.
verdict.audience: Localised intermediate-risk prostate, definitive RT, median age 68

studies.significance: The efficacy caution sits in the secondary data: 3yr cumulative biochemical failure was 8% (5.2-11.0) with SBRT vs 4% (2.3-7.0) with IMRT, p=0.037, under a QoL-positive headline. The bowel benefit came with mandated fiducials, MRI fusion, daily IGRT, 5 mm/3 mm PTV margins and a spacer in 56%, which is the setup a department has to reproduce.
studies.monday_clinic: In a man with localised intermediate-risk disease weighing 5 fractions against 20 to 28, this supports SBRT on bowel and continence grounds while flagging the higher 3yr biochemical failure rate; it does not extend to high-risk, node-positive, or post-prostatectomy settings.

primary_endpoint.name: EPIC-26 bowel MCID decline at 24 months (co-primary)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: SBRT vs MH-IMRT, p=0.034; DFS co-primary crossed futility, HR 1.38

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Randomised, non-blinded phase 3, 1:1, **N=698** (SBRT 353, MH-IMRT 345), stratified by Gleason score, PSA and rectal manipulation, with one interim futility analysis per endpoint. The DFS analysis was sized at **178 events from 590 evaluable pts** for 89% power; target accrual was 691.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Localised **intermediate-risk** prostate cancer, median age 68 (IMRT) and 69 (SBRT). Baseline EPIC domains were balanced (bowel 96.3 vs 96.0, p=0.69; urinary irritation 89.4 vs 89.7, p=0.78). **Rectal spacer in 56% SBRT vs 55% IMRT.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions** of 7.25 Gy, 2 to 3 fractions per week, PTV expansion 5 mm radially and 3 mm posteriorly and anteriorly, max PTV dose 38.8 Gy. **MH-IMRT 70 Gy/28 fx or 60 Gy/20 fx**, expansion 8 mm except 5 mm posteriorly. CTV was prostate ±1 cm proximal seminal vesicles in both arms.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary:** EPIC-26 bowel and urinary irritative/obstructive MCID at 24 months (thresholds ≥4 and ≥5 points), and **disease-free survival** (Phoenix biochemical failure, local, regional, distant failure, or death). HRQOL was powered for 10% and 8% absolute reductions in MCID frequency; DFS assumed HR 0.62.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Bowel co-primary met**, urinary irritative co-primary flat, DFS co-primary crossed its interim futility bound (see endpoint table). Longitudinal modelling favored SBRT for bowel (LS mean 2.68, 95% CI 1.02-4.34, p=0.0016) and urinary incontinence (2.91, 95% CI 0.85-4.97, p=0.0058); sexual and hormonal domains showed no treatment effect.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Investigator-graded toxicity ran in SBRT's favor across grade ≥3 GU, any-grade rectal hemorrhage and any-grade fatigue (see table). Reporting in the source is cross-sectional, with **no late-effect breakdown** beyond rectal hemorrhage.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PACE-B is the other large randomised comparison of SBRT with MH-IMRT, and the **urinary incontinence advantage reproduces there** despite differing MCID definitions. MH-IMRT's standing rests on RTOG 0415 and its long-term update, so the comparator arm is the schedule with the longest track record, not a straw man.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localised intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with definitive prostate-only RT under mandated fiducials, MRI-based planning and daily IGRT. Does not represent high-risk or node-positive disease, elective pelvic coverage, or post-prostatectomy salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Non-blinded with patient-reported co-primaries, so assignment to a 5-visit course can bias reporting toward SBRT. Pre-treatment attrition was asymmetric (**22 IMRT pts vs 1 SBRT pt never received assigned RT**), and 2yr EPIC completion was 82.5% vs 85.1%. Biochemical control is read off an interim analysis and stays immature.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Local and distant failures were few in both arms, so the disease-control separation rests on **early biochemical events**, an endpoint prone to reclassification with longer follow-up in intermediate-risk disease. The trial makes SBRT defensible on the HRQOL grounds it was adopted for, without settling whether the two schedules are equivalent for cure.

studies.interpretation:
This trial answers a question the field had already half-answered by adoption. Five-fraction SBRT spread on the strength of single-arm series and patient-level pooled analyses of patient-reported outcomes; NRG-GU005 set out to prove it superior on both toxicity and disease control, and it returns a split result that should be read as two separate findings rather than one.

On the patient-reported side the result is internally consistent. Fewer men on SBRT crossed the bowel MCID threshold at one and two years, urinary incontinence declines were less frequent at two years, and investigator-graded grade 3 or higher GU events and any-grade rectal hemorrhage both ran higher with IMRT. The urinary incontinence signal is the one that also appears in PACE-B, the only other large randomised comparison of these two schedules, though the two trials defined MCID slightly differently. That concordance carries the argument, because the obvious threat to a patient-reported endpoint in an unblinded trial is expectation: men randomised to five treatments over two weeks know they drew the shorter course, and that bias pushes in exactly the direction the result went. Agreement with investigator-graded toxicity is what makes the bowel finding believable, more than the p-value does.

The efficacy side deserves more caution than the take-home slide suggests. Disease-free survival crossed a futility bound with a hazard ratio pointing away from SBRT, and cumulative biochemical failure at three years was 8% with SBRT against 4% with IMRT. Neither observation establishes inferiority: the trial was built to detect a 38% relative improvement, it stopped for futility rather than harm, and the interval around the hazard ratio is compatible with no difference. But a superiority trial that stops early leaves the non-inferiority question formally unasked, and a reader who has been treating the two schedules as interchangeable has been assuming an answer this trial did not supply. Three-year biochemical failure in intermediate-risk disease is an early read on a slow endpoint, and whether the curves converge, separate further, or partly reflect PSA behaviour after 7.25 Gy per fraction will not be settled without longer follow-up.

Transferability is the other thing to hold onto. This was not permissive SBRT. Fiducials, MRI fusion for planning and daily image guidance were mandated, PTV expansions were 5 mm radially and 3 mm anteriorly and posteriorly, and a rectal spacer was used in 56% of the SBRT arm, with spacer use itself associated with better bowel scores. A department delivering 36.25 Gy in five fractions without that infrastructure is not delivering the intervention that produced these numbers, and the bowel advantage is the part most likely to erode first.

What changes in clinic is narrow and real: for a man with intermediate-risk disease who weighs bowel and continence outcomes and five visits heavily, the choice now rests on randomised evidence rather than pooled series. What does not change is the standing of moderate hypofractionation, which is the arm with the numerically better biochemical control here and the schedule with the longer track record from RTOG 0415 onward.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Fractionation, not coverage, is what moved: CTV was prostate ±1 cm proximal seminal vesicles in both arms, so differing elective volumes cannot explain the 8% vs 4% 3yr biochemical failure gap. Five fractions buys bowel and continence, delivered with 5 mm/3 mm margins, daily IGRT and a spacer in 56%.

open_questions: Whether the 3yr biochemical failure gap persists with longer follow-up
Which intermediate-risk subgroups drive the biochemical failure difference
Whether the SBRT bowel benefit holds without a rectal spacer

sites.intro: ESTRO fills the post-op CTV gap with geometry, not outcome data.

studies.name: ESTRO CTV Delineation Guidelines (Post-op OCSCC)
studies.tldr: First consensus post-op CTV atlas for oral cavity SCC: CTV-P = GTV-P pre-op + 10 mm composited with surgical defect/flap + 5 mm.
details: 🔍 ESTRO multidisciplinary expert group; no consensus guideline previously existed for post-op CTV delineation in mucosal HNSCC

subdetails: Step 1a: re-create GTV-P pre-op on diagnostic MRI/CT, edit on planning CT
Step 1b: delineate surgical defect (no reconstruction) or flap body (reconstructed)
Step 2b: surgical defect/flap + 5 mm isotropic, added independently
Step 2c: CTV-P = union of both, edited for bone, fascia, air, intra-oral prosthesis

details.text: 📐 10 mm justified from surgical series: microscopic infiltration within 5 mm of GTV-P edge in >95% of resected OCSCC
🔍 Nodal margin depends on pENE status, not level anatomy alone
subdetails: No pENE: GTV-N pre-op + 5 mm, composited with involved level(s) and post-op change → CTV-N1
pENE: GTV-N pre-op + 10 mm → CTV-N high-risk
Nodes not identifiable pre-op or poor co-registration: outline whole involved level(s) + seroma/clips instead

details.text: 🔍 When PORT to the neck can be omitted (adequate ≥18 node dissection)
subdetails: pN0 after adequate dissection: neck PORT generally not required
pN1 after adequate dissection: may not be required; single node >10 mm but ≤30 mm is an indication
Single node ≤10 mm: adjuvant RT not routinely recommended
PORT indicated in neck but not primary: still treat both, to cover T-N tract and lingual nodes

details: 🔗 Extends the 2018 definitive-setting HNSCC CTV guideline's 5 + 5 mm geometric expansion into the post-op setting
🔗 GORTEC 2020 flap delineation guidance cited as a useful adjunct for standardising flap outlining
⚠️ Consensus + expert opinion, no outcome data: no recurrence, toxicity or dosimetric endpoint tests these margins
⚠️ Whether central flap body can be dose-de-escalated is explicitly unresolved; a flap avoidance structure is offered without supporting data
⚠️ Dose to dissected uninvolved levels left to clinician discretion, resting on a 1993 MD Anderson observation never tested prospectively

verdict.rationale: ESTRO expert guideline with international external review; output is a delineation method and dose allocation, no efficacy endpoint. First post-op CTV consensus in mucosal HNSCC.
verdict.audience: Resected oral cavity SCC receiving post-operative RT

studies.significance: The load-bearing recommendation is asymmetric: 10 mm around a re-created pre-op GTV, only 5 mm around the surgical defect or flap, unioned rather than nested. Fig 3.1/3.2 show why the GTV-P step is not optional, the pre-op tumour extended superiorly beyond the defect into the infratemporal fossa, a geographical miss if the defect alone had been used.
studies.monday_clinic: For a resected OCSCC patient going to PORT, this supports carrying the pre-operative MRI-defined tumour onto the planning CT as a target-defining volume rather than contouring the surgical bed alone; it does not address whether that patient needs PORT, or extend to R2 resections or other head and neck subsites.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO-convened multidisciplinary expert group (radiation oncology, surgery, pathology, radiology). Guidelines developed by discussion and review of current evidence and international practice, then externally reviewed by HNSCC experts from countries outside the authorship (Japan, Hong Kong, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Canada, Denmark, France, Spain, Poland, Ireland, UK) and modified on their feedback. **No formal Delphi round or quantified agreement statistic is reported.**

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Patients with **oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma** requiring post-operative radiotherapy. Applies **regardless of margin status and other histological risk factors**. **R2 resection (macroscopic residual disease) is explicitly out of scope.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Supine, neutral neck, custom immobilisation; **2.0 mm (range 1-3 mm) CT slices** skull base to below the sterno-clavicular joint with **mandatory IV contrast**. Rigid co-registration of pre-operative contrast CT and/or MRI, matched to **C1-C3 vertebrae or nearby bone (mandible, hard palate)**, never to soft tissue, which surgery has moved. CTV-P = **(GTV-P pre-op + 10 mm) + (defect or flap + 5 mm)**, edited for bone, fascia, air, prosthesis; nodal margin is **5 mm without pENE, 10 mm with pENE**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: None. The deliverable is a delineation method plus a nodal-level allocation table, not a measured outcome. Stated aim is consistency across institutions, enabling **multi-institutional audit, clinical trials and RTQA**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents resected OCSCC of any subsite going to PORT, including flap-reconstructed necks and pENE. Does not represent R2 resections, non-oral-cavity HNSCC subsites, or the re-irradiation setting.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Directly extends the 2018 international definitive-setting CTV guideline, whose **5 + 5 mm geometric expansion** becomes the 10 mm here. Supporting evidence for geometric over anatomical margins is indirect: DAHANCA showed geometric expansion gives more conformal CTVs, and an **unplanned post-hoc analysis of De-ESCALaTE** correlated the anatomical-to-geometric protocol change with lower late dysphagia. Dutch non-randomised series reducing the high-risk margin from **10 mm to 6 mm** reported lower salivary and constrictor dose and lower toxicity versus historical controls, so the 10 mm chosen here is not the only defensible number in the definitive setting.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The margins are anchored to a single surgical-pathology observation (**microscopic infiltration within 5 mm in >95% of resected cases**) applied to a post-operative bed whose geometry has already been altered by resection and flap inset. Re-creating GTV-P pre-op depends on co-registration quality; where that fails the guideline falls back to examination notes, photographs and operative findings, which is exactly the unquantified inter-observer variability these guidelines exist to reduce.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The genuinely new claim is that the pre-operative tumour, not the surgical bed, carries information the bed has lost. Two worked cases make it concrete: a buccal mucosa tumour extending superiorly past the defect into the infratemporal fossa, and an ill-defined buccal fat pad reconstruction the fibrotic bed cannot delineate. Whether this reduces marginal recurrence, or merely enlarges volumes, is untested.

studies.interpretation:
The argument this guideline actually makes is narrower and more interesting than "here are some margins." It is that the post-operative bed is an unreliable surrogate for the tissue at risk, and that a re-created pre-operative GTV should be carried forward into the planning scan as a second, independent surrogate. Everything else follows from that: the two expansions are generated separately and unioned, not nested, precisely because neither volume alone reliably contains the other. The worked cases are the evidence offered, and they are chosen to make the failure mode visible rather than to quantify it. A right upper buccal mucosa tumour extended superiorly beyond its surgical defect toward the infratemporal fossa; a buccal fat pad reconstruction was too ill-defined on planning CT to outline with confidence. In both, defect-only or flap-only contouring produces a geographical miss that no margin recipe applied to the wrong starting volume would recover.

The numeric choices are inherited rather than derived. The 10 mm around GTV-P pre-op is the 5 + 5 mm expansion from the 2018 definitive-setting guideline, itself justified by the surgical observation that microscopic infiltration lies within 5 mm of the GTV edge in more than 95% of resected OCSCC. Importing it into the post-operative setting requires an assumption the document does not test: that a bed already resected with a margin, then reconstructed, has the same microscopic risk geometry as an intact tumour. The 5 mm around the defect or flap is the softer number, presented as sufficient rather than validated. It is worth noting the definitive setting is itself in motion here. Dutch non-randomised work cited in the introduction reduced the high-risk margin from 10 mm to 6 mm and reported lower salivary and constrictor doses with lower acute and late toxicity against historical controls. A guideline whose parent margin is under active de-escalation elsewhere is inheriting a number that may not stay fixed.

What should move a reader's confidence upward is the process and the failure-mode reasoning; what should move it down is the complete absence of an outcome endpoint. There is no recurrence rate, no dosimetric comparison against current practice, no inter-observer variability statistic before and after. The supporting evidence for geometric over anatomical margins is real but indirect: DAHANCA conformality data, and a post-hoc analysis of De-ESCALaTE correlating a protocol change with lower late dysphagia. That is a reasonable basis for standardising a method. It is not a basis for asserting the standardised method improves control.

The honest read is that this changes contouring practice and leaves treatment decisions untouched. Indications for PORT come from the companion background manuscript, not here, and the nodal table largely codifies existing practice around adequate dissection and pENE. Where the document does something quietly consequential is dose allocation at the boundary: dissected but uninvolved levels are left to clinician discretion at 50 to 60 Gy, resting on a 1993 MD Anderson rationale about perturbed, potentially hypoxic tissue that has never been tested prospectively. That is a candid admission, and it marks the place where standardisation stops. For the reader who adopts this, the practical consequence is that volumes will likely grow, particularly in flap-reconstructed cases where the composite extends beyond the oral cavity and must be trimmed by clinical judgement rather than rule. Whether that trade lands as fewer marginal misses or more xerostomia is exactly what the prospective audits the authors call for would have to answer.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The asymmetric margins are the operational content: 10 mm around a re-created GTV-P pre-op, 5 mm around the defect or flap, unioned not nested. Fig 3.1/3.2 show a case where the pre-op tumour extended superiorly past the defect into the infratemporal fossa, so skipping the GTV-P step is a geographical miss, not a simplification.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The guideline makes the operative record part of the radiotherapy target: pan-endoscopy findings, clinical photographs, intra-operative findings and the localisation of a positive margin all feed delineation, and surgeon input is requested in complex cases. Marking a <1mm margin with a surgical clip lets that area alone take EQD2 64-66 Gy rather than the whole CTV-P.

open_questions: Does dose de-escalation to the central flap body compromise control?
Optimal dose to dissected but uninvolved nodal levels
Do these margins reduce marginal recurrence or only enlarge volumes?
